title: What Interviewers Actually Ask IB Applicants
summary: Learn what university interviewers ask IB applicants, how to discuss your EE, TOK, CAS and HL subjects, and how to prepare effectively in fall.
body_markdown:
University interviewers do not usually have questions reserved specifically for IB students. They ask about your academic interests, course choice, application evidence, relevant experiences and ability to respond thoughtfully to unfamiliar ideas. Your **Higher Level subjects** , **Extended Essay** , **Internal Assessments** , **TOK** and **CAS** matter because they provide strong examples for answering those questions.


The exact content depends on the institution, course and interview format. An Oxford or Cambridge academic interview differs substantially from a US alumni conversation, while medicine, dentistry and creative courses may use structured stations, portfolios or auditions.


### First identify the interview format


Before preparing answers, check the university admissions page and your invitation for the format, length, platform and assessment purpose.


Interview type Main focus Typical task


Academic or tutorial-style Subject reasoning and response to new ideas Analyse a text, graph, problem or unfamiliar source


Conversational or alumni Curiosity, experiences and institutional fit Discuss motivations, interests and university life


Panel Course suitability and communication Answer structured questions from several interviewers


Multiple Mini Interview Professional judgement and interpersonal skills Complete ethical, teamwork or role-play stations


Portfolio or audition Creative process and technical potential Explain work, perform or respond to criticism


Oxford describes interviews as subject conversations resembling short tutorials. Candidates may receive an unfamiliar poem, graph, object or problem and work through it aloud.[Cambridge interview guidance](https://www.undergraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/apply/after/cambridge-interviews) similarly explains that applicants may apply existing knowledge to new situations.


Conversational interviews serve a different purpose.[Yale states that its interviews](https://admissions.yale.edu/interviews) are evaluative but not required, while MIT describes its alumni interview as an informal conversation that adds context to the application. An invitation does not automatically mean you are facing an oral examination.


### Questions interviewers ask IB applicants


### Why do you want to study this subject?


This tests how your interest developed, not how enthusiastically you can praise the subject. Identify a specific starting point, explain what you explored next and connect that exploration to what you want to study.


A psychology applicant might connect an HL lesson on memory with an independent article, an IA design choice and a question about eyewitness testimony. This demonstrates curiosity through action rather than simply claiming that psychology is fascinating.


### Why this university or course?


Discuss current curriculum features, teaching methods, placements, research opportunities or interdisciplinary options that match your interests. Avoid relying on rankings, reputation or location.


For example, explain how a first-year laboratory sequence would develop skills introduced by your Biology IA. Confirm every detail on the current course page before mentioning it.


### What have you studied recently that interested you?


Interviewers may ask what evidence supports an idea, what its limitations are, how it connects with another topic or whether your opinion has changed. Review important concepts from your HL subjects and practise explaining them clearly. The goal is not to predict one perfect topic, but to distinguish evidence from assumption and remain thoughtful when challenged.


### Tell me about your Extended Essay


Prepare your research question, method, main conclusion, greatest limitation and one decision you would change. Do not recite the abstract. A useful structure is: I investigated a question, used a particular method, reached a qualified conclusion and identified a limitation.


The[RevisionDojo guide to using your EE in university applications](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-do-i-use-my-ee-topic-in-college-applications) explains how to turn the project into a concise academic narrative.


### What did TOK or CAS teach you?


Interviewers rarely need a textbook definition of TOK. They may instead ask how you evaluate evidence, handle uncertainty or compare conflicting interpretations. Apply TOK habits naturally without forcing IB vocabulary into every response.


CAS is useful when discussing teamwork, service, leadership, conflict or failure. Since CAS is an IB requirement, completion alone is not distinctive. Explain your responsibility, decisions, contribution and reflection, as recommended in the[RevisionDojo guide to IB applications in the US](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-in-college-apps-us) .


### Unfamiliar academic and professional questions


Academic interviews often move quickly beyond personal questions. Possible materials include:


- **Mathematics and sciences:** multistep problems, graphs, experimental results or unfamiliar applications of known principles
- **Humanities:** sources, images, quotations, poems or arguments requiring interpretation
- **Social sciences:** datasets, policy problems, case studies or competing explanations
- **Medicine:** communication tasks, ethical scenarios, teamwork and professional judgement
- **Creative subjects:** portfolio choices, influences, revisions and responses to criticism


The[Medical Schools Council interview guidance](https://www.medschools.ac.uk/for-students/applying-to-medical-school/interviews/) distinguishes panel interviews, Multiple Mini Interviews and assessment centres. Always prepare for the format named by the individual medical school.


When answering an unfamiliar question:


1. **Clarify the task** if a term or instruction is unclear.
2. **State what you notice** , including patterns, evidence and assumptions.
3. **Connect the material** to a relevant concept or method.
4. **Think aloud** so the interviewer can follow your reasoning.
5. **Use prompts** as additional information rather than signs of failure.
6. **Revise your conclusion** when the evidence justifies a change.


If a graph contradicts your prediction, identify the discrepancy and reconsider your assumptions. Intellectual flexibility is usually more valuable than defending an unsupported first answer.


### Questions about setbacks and pressure


A challenge question does not require a dramatic hardship story. Interviewers usually want evidence of self-awareness, responsibility and improvement.


You might discuss narrowing an overambitious EE question, redesigning an IA method or responding to disappointing mock results. Use **situation, action, result, reflection** , spending most of the answer on what you controlled and changed.


### A September-November preparation plan


### September: build an evidence bank


Prepare six examples from your EE, an IA, TOK, CAS, an academic setback and an independent interest. For each, record your role, action, learning and one likely follow-up question. Use a[global IB university application checklist](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-apply-to-university-as-an-ib-student-step-by-step-guide-for-global-admissions) to confirm which institutions actually interview.


### October: practise academic explanation


Reread submitted application materials and verify every book, article, project and course feature mentioned. Ask a teacher to challenge an academic claim rather than only asking generic personal questions. The[RevisionDojo guide to UCAS assessment](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-universities-assess-ucas-applications) helps place interviews alongside predicted grades, references, tests and written work.


### November: simulate the real format


Complete two or three realistic practices rather than repeatedly rehearsing scripts. For online interviews, test your microphone, camera, internet connection and method for displaying mathematical working.[UCAS interview advice](https://www.ucas.com/applying/after-you-apply/undergraduate-interview-invitations) also recommends checking arrangements, practising aloud and preparing questions.


### Common preparation mistakes


- Memorising complete scripts that collapse under follow-up questions
- Listing IB activities without explaining decisions or reflection
- Forgetting that submitted application material may be discussed
- Bluffing instead of acknowledging uncertainty and reasoning carefully
- Giving generic praise based on prestige or rankings
- Preparing for an Oxbridge interview when the actual format is conversational, professional or portfolio-based
- Using AI-generated wording that does not reflect your genuine experience


### What to ask the interviewer


Prepare two or three questions that are not answered easily on the university homepage. Ask about progression into independent research, feedback in small-group teaching or opportunities to combine academic interests. Direct questions about admissions conditions, visas or documentation to the admissions office rather than an alumnus.


### Conclusion


What interviewers ask IB applicants depends mainly on the course and format, but common themes include subject motivation, academic curiosity, communication, reflection and responsiveness to new evidence. Prepare themes rather than scripts, practise explaining ideas aloud and follow each institution's current instructions.


RevisionDojo **Study Notes** and the **Questionbank** can refresh subject knowledge. Jojo AI or a RevisionDojo Tutor can provide follow-up prompts and help you practise concise, authentic explanations.
